points.title: What a prototype is
points.must: An early, simplified working model of a new system (or part of it) that shows how it will look and behave, so users can try it and give feedback before the full system is built.

points.title: Prototyping
points.must: Developing a system by building a prototype, letting users test it and refining it in repeated cycles until the users are satisfied.

points.title: The prototyping cycle
points.must: The steps in order: identify basic requirements → build prototype → users test → collect feedback → satisfied? No: refine and test again; Yes: build the final system (a diagram or list), with a note that it is iterative.

points.title: What a prototype includes and leaves out
points.must: Includes screens, navigation, input forms and reports with example data; usually leaves out full data storage, security, backups and speed.

points.title: Where it fits in the life cycle
points.must: Prototypes are built and refined during analysis and design, before the full system is coded.

points.title: Throw-away prototype
points.must: Built quickly and cheaply only to find out / agree the requirements, then discarded; the real system is built from scratch.

points.title: Evolutionary prototype
points.must: Improved step by step, version after version, until it becomes the final system.

points.title: Throw-away vs evolutionary
points.must: A comparison of at least two features: purpose, what happens to it, speed of building, code quality, when it is best used.

points.title: Low- and high-fidelity
points.must: Low-fidelity = paper sketches / wireframes, cheap, shows layout; high-fidelity = looks and behaves almost like the real system (Figma, HTML).

points.title: Horizontal and vertical prototypes
points.must: Horizontal = many screens of the whole system with little working behind them (wide, shallow); vertical = one function built completely down to the database (narrow, deep), with an example of each.

points.title: Advantages of prototyping
points.must: At least four: missing requirements found early; quick user feedback; better understanding between users and developers; errors fixed early so time and cost are reduced; users feel involved and accept the system; used for training / user guide.

points.title: Disadvantages of prototyping
points.must: At least four: additional development cost; time-consuming; users think it is the finished system; scope creep (endless change requests); constrains the designer's ideas; hides real complexity; poorly structured code if kept.

points.title: Why the total cost can fall
points.must: Errors and missing requirements are found before coding, when they are much cheaper to fix than after development or go-live (cost-of-fixing diagram or explanation).

points.title: Point plus effect
points.must: At least one advantage or disadvantage written as a 'because … so …' chain, e.g. users test the form early, so missing fields are added before coding.

points.title: Scenario judgement
points.must: A worked decision for a scenario (e.g. bakery or clinic) on whether to build a prototype, with a reason for and against and a conclusion.
